# Does "bumping" up and down a kerb damage my car?

If your driveway lacks a dropped kerb, daily driving over a 7cm obstruction is an inevitable part of your routine. The core question is whether this repetitive impact degrades suspension components or wears out tyres prematurely. The short answer is that while occasional use is negligible, high-frequency operation at speed introduces measurable stress factors that can accelerate component fatigue.

## Suspension Dynamics and Impact Loads

When a vehicle transitions over a vertical obstacle, the suspension must absorb the kinetic energy of the mass striking the ground. A 7cm kerb represents a significant step change in elevation compared to standard road irregularities like potholes or speed bumps. The severity of the impact depends heavily on velocity.

At a slow crawl (under 3 mph), the suspension has sufficient time to compress and rebound through its full travel range, effectively isolating the cabin and chassis from the shock. However, increasing speedâeven to 5 mph as mentionedâincreases the vertical velocity vector at the moment of contact. This forces the dampers (shock absorbers) to work harder within a shorter timeframe.

Dampers are designed to control oscillation, not just absorb energy. Repeatedly forcing a damper past its optimal operating point can lead to fluid aeration or seal wear over time. If the suspension components are already worn, such as bushings with excessive play or struts nearing the end of their service life, the impact forces will be transmitted directly to the chassis rails and wheel bearings rather than being absorbed by the hydraulic system.

## Tyre Wear Patterns

The interaction between the tyre and the kerb affects tread life in specific ways. When driving up a kerb, the front wheels act as levers. If the kerb is sharp-edged (common with concrete curbs), it can bite into the sidewall if the suspension allows the wheel to drop significantly after impact. This "chewing" of the sidewall compromises structural integrity and increases the risk of a blowout under heavy load.

More subtly, repeated impacts alter tread wear patterns. The side of the tyre facing the kerb experiences uneven friction and compression. Over thousands of cycles, this can lead to cupping or scalloping on the outer edge of the contact patch. While modern tyres are durable, consistent driving over a fixed vertical obstacle acts as a form of localized abrasion that reduces overall tread life faster than normal highway driving.

## Engineering Trade-offs and Mitigation

There is no software fix or setting adjustment in your vehicle to mitigate this mechanical reality. The physics of impact remains constant regardless of the brand or model. However, regular maintenance can extend the lifespan of components subjected to this specific stress vector.

Inspecting suspension bushings and ball joints more frequently than standard intervals is advisable. If these mounting points show signs of cracking or excessive play, replacing them before failure becomes imminent is a prudent engineering decision. Similarly, monitoring tyre pressure is critical; under-inflated tyres are more susceptible to sidewall damage when climbing kerbs because the rubber flexes more violently against the concrete edge.

If the frequency of this operation makes you concerned about long-term reliability, the most effective solution remains installing a dropped kerb. This modifies the physical interface between the road and the vehicle, eliminating the vertical delta that causes the impact shock in the first place. From an engineering standpoint, removing the load path is always superior to relying on component durability under repeated overload conditions.
